lessons.title: Finding the main idea
lessons.hook: A paragraph can have several pictures in it and still make one point.
lessons.idea: Name the topic, then say what the writer wants you to understand about it.

scenes.show: Three cards show traffic, dirt and a thought coming back. The cards slide towards the same line.
scenes.say: Look at the passage about thoughts. Find the part with traffic and dirt. The writer is not giving advice about a busy road. Read the words around those pictures. They show what can happen when a person keeps thinking the same harmful thoughts.

beats.action: Group the examples under harmful thoughts.
beats.label: Group the examples under harmful thoughts

scenes.show: The label Thoughts appears, then a second line grows underneath it.
scenes.say: First name the topic in a few words. Here the topic is harmful thoughts. Now ask what the writer says about them. The writer says they can grow stronger when we keep them in mind. That second part tells us the main idea.

beats.action: Join the topic and the point.
beats.label: Join the topic and the point

scenes.show: One picture card stays lit. Then highlights on sentences 13 to 16 light together.
scenes.say: Try covering one example. The sentence about traffic can disappear and the point still holds. Now put it back. It fits the same point as the other examples. A main idea should cover the examples together. A detail usually explains just one.

beats.action: Show that the same idea fits every example.
beats.label: Show that the same idea fits every example

scenes.show: A short and a narrow answer appear side by side. The narrow answer fades.
scenes.say: Before you look at the choices, say the point in your own words. Use plain language. Then compare it with the answers on the page. Cross out any choice that treats an image as a fact about real traffic or real house guests.

beats.action: Reveal the choices after the learner forms a summary.
beats.label: Reveal the choices after the learner forms a summary

misconception.wrong: The most striking example must be the main idea.
misconception.correction: A main idea explains why the examples are there.

pastQuestion.prompt: which of the following statement summarizes the argument of the fourth paragraph
options: heavy traffic on a miry and dirty road may lead to evil thoughts
the more evil we think, the more vile we are likely to become
evil people should not be welcome as guest in our homes the same way we welcome good people
evil thoughts control the key to human heart and no one can keep them out

scenes.show: Reveal JAMB 2011 Q10 and the printed options beside sentences 13 to 16.
scenes.say: This is JAMB twenty eleven, question ten. It asks which choice sums up the argument of the fourth paragraph. Follow the images of busy traffic, dirt and an imagination that can get back in. Together they show that a harmful thought grows when it is indulged.

beats.action: Keep the examples together as the narration names their shared point.
beats.label: Keep the examples together as the narration names their shared point

scenes.show: Highlight sentences 13 to 16 at the cue, then light option B.
scenes.say: Look at sentences thirteen to sixteen. The answer is here. A makes the road real. C changes thoughts into visitors. D goes too far and says they cannot be kept out. B keeps the writer's point about the effect of thinking this way again and again. Choose B.

beats.action: Highlight proof sentences 13 to 16.
beats.label: Highlight proof sentences 13 to 16

lessons.syllabus: Read the passage closely and use its evidence to answer the question.

lessons.title: Literal versus inference questions
lessons.hook: Find one answer the writer gives you directly and one idea you can work out from a clue.
lessons.idea: Literal questions ask what the passage says directly. Inference questions ask for a conclusion the clues support.

scenes.show: Place a question card above numbered sentences and highlight the words how and size.
scenes.say: Look at the story about making pots in Abuja. If a question asks how the potter keeps the pots the same size, underline how and size. These words tell you what to look for. You want a step the writer gives you in the passage.

beats.action: Underline the idea the answer must contain.
beats.label: Underline the idea the answer must contain

scenes.show: Sentence 9 lights up. A scale appears beside the words weighed out.
scenes.say: A literal answer can be pointed to. Sentence nine tells us that the lumps of clay are weighed out so each pot will be roughly the same size. The answer choice may use different words. The meaning must still be the same as the line.

beats.action: Highlight the action and its reason.
beats.label: Highlight the action and its reason

scenes.show: Show two equal lumps on a scale and an arrow leading to equal jugs.
scenes.say: An inference takes one extra step. Suppose you ask why the potter would weigh two lumps before shaping them. The text links the amount of clay to the size of the pot. From that link you can work out what might happen if the lumps differ greatly.

beats.action: Show the clue and the conclusion separately.
beats.label: Show the clue and the conclusion separately

scenes.show: Cross out a crack icon. Keep the scale and equally sized pots in view.
scenes.say: Test a guess by asking which line makes it likely. You might guess that pots made this way will never crack. Look for a line that supports that idea. This passage explains speed, accuracy and size. The claim about cracking has no evidence, so cross it out.

beats.action: Erase the guess without evidence.
beats.label: Erase the guess without evidence

misconception.wrong: An inference is any guess that sounds possible.
misconception.correction: An inference needs evidence from the passage.

pastQuestion.prompt: From the passage, how does a potter make several pots of almost identical size?
options: By having the knowledge of different pots.
By weighing the lumps of clay.
By knowing what to do from experience.

scenes.show: Reveal JAMB 2013 Q3. Display the four printed options with sentence 9.
scenes.say: This is JAMB twenty thirteen, question three. It asks how the potter makes several pots of almost identical size. Find the phrase roughly the same size in sentence nine. Check the action just before it. The writer tells you the method directly, so you do not need to infer it.

beats.action: Point from the question to the stated method.
beats.label: Point from the question to the stated method

scenes.show: Highlight sentence 9 at the cue and reveal answer B.
scenes.say: Read the first part of sentence nine. The answer is here. The potter weighs the lumps of clay. The right tools and experience may help a potter in general, but neither is the step named for keeping pots the same size. Choose B.

beats.action: Highlight proof sentence 9.
beats.label: Highlight proof sentence 9

lessons.syllabus: Read the passage closely and use its evidence to answer the question.

lessons.title: Word meaning from context
lessons.hook: Read around an expression before deciding what it means in that passage.
lessons.idea: Context includes what happens before and after a word or phrase.

scenes.show: Show the words rock the boat, first with a boat icon, then beside a classroom.
scenes.say: Look at the words rock the boat in the passage about the geography master. If you see the phrase alone, you may picture water. Go back to the sentence. It takes place after a boy has challenged the master in class. Read for what changes in that room.

beats.action: Move from the literal picture to the classroom.
beats.label: Move from the literal picture to the classroom

scenes.show: Reveal sentences 14 to 16. The master exits and the class turns towards the boy.
scenes.say: Read the lines before the expression. The master gives the boy an angry look and leaves. Then the other pupils blame the boy. The boy has upset the usual order of the class. These reactions help you understand the expression without needing to know it in advance.

beats.action: Link the clues to what the boy did.
beats.label: Link the clues to what the boy did

scenes.show: Replace rock the boat temporarily with upset the usual order, then restore the printed words.
scenes.say: Try a plain substitute for the expression. Say that the boy upset the usual order. Put that meaning back into the sentence and see if the story still makes sense. If you try become a sailor instead, the idea will not fit anything that has happened in the classroom.

beats.action: Test the replacement against the situation.
beats.label: Test the replacement against the situation

scenes.show: Show the four figure-of-speech labels. The direct comparison lights up.
scenes.say: When the question asks for the figure of speech, look at how the phrase works. The writer describes one situation through another. The writer does not say it is like a rocking boat. The phrase calls the disturbance rocking the boat, which makes it a metaphor.

beats.action: Connect the phrase and its label.
beats.label: Connect the phrase and its label

misconception.wrong: An expression always means what its words describe literally.
misconception.correction: Read the action around the phrase and test the meaning that fits.

pastQuestion.prompt: "...rock the boat" What figure of speech is this expression?

scenes.show: Reveal JAMB 2018 Q3 with its four printed options and scroll to sentence 16.
scenes.say: This is JAMB twenty eighteen, question three. It asks what figure of speech the expression rock the boat uses. Remember the boy is in a classroom. He questions a claim the master often makes. His challenge upsets the class, which is why people turn their anger on him.

beats.action: Keep the classroom action beside the expression.
beats.label: Keep the classroom action beside the expression

scenes.show: Highlight sentence 16 at the cue and then reveal answer B.
scenes.say: Look at sentence sixteen. The answer is here. The boat is a picture for the usual order, and rocking it means upsetting that order. There is no like or as in the expression to make it a simile. The sentence gives a metaphor. Choose B.

beats.action: Highlight proof sentence 16.
beats.label: Highlight proof sentence 16

lessons.syllabus: Read the passage closely and use its evidence to answer the question.

lessons.title: Cloze and summary
lessons.hook: Use words next to a gap to fill it. Use the whole passage to make a summary.
lessons.idea: A gap needs a local clue. A summary needs the main point of the wider passage.

scenes.show: Open the cloze passage and place a blank in sentence 15 while the surrounding words brighten.
scenes.say: A cloze passage has numbered gaps. Read the words just before and after a gap. Start there, because those words can tell you whether you need a name, an action or a describing word. The best choice must make sense and fit the sentence when you read it aloud.

beats.action: Light the words on both sides of the blank.
beats.label: Light the words on both sides of the blank

scenes.show: Light the plural noun after the blank, then underline the example such as twins.
scenes.say: Look at the gap before pregnancies in the last sentence. The missing word describes the pregnancies. The phrase such as twins gives you an example. Use that example to decide what sort of word would fit. Try each choice in place and see whether the example explains it.

beats.action: Connect the example to the blank.
beats.label: Connect the example to the blank

scenes.show: Zoom out to show the passage. Group definition, signs and risk as three lines.
scenes.say: A summary uses more of the passage. Read the opening to find the topic. Then look at what later sentences add. This passage gives a definition, describes signs and discusses risk. Those groups tell you what the passage is doing better than a single example such as twins does.

beats.action: Group the sentences by what each adds.
beats.label: Group the sentences by what each adds

scenes.show: The three groups roll into a one-sentence summary while example cards fade.
scenes.say: Say the summary in one sentence. The passage defines miscarriage and describes its signs and factors linked with risk. That covers the groups we marked. You can leave out individual examples. The gap question still needs its own clue, so return to the sentence before choosing an answer.

beats.action: Keep the summary visible as the gap sentence returns.
beats.label: Keep the summary visible as the gap sentence returns

misconception.wrong: One word can settle both the gap and the summary.
misconception.correction: Test the gap in its sentence, then read across the passage for the summary.

pastQuestion.prompt: It is also increased with ...25... pregnancies such as twins.

scenes.show: Reveal JAMB 2012 Q25 and read the four printed options beside sentence 15.
scenes.say: This is JAMB twenty twelve, question twenty-five. It asks for the word in the final gap. Read the sentence through the blank. The words pregnancies such as twins show us the writer is giving an example. We need a describing word that explains what distinguishes twins.

beats.action: Underline such as twins.
beats.label: Underline such as twins

scenes.show: Highlight sentence 15 on the cue and fill the gap with multiple.
scenes.say: Read the end of sentence fifteen again. The answer is here. Twins means more than one baby. Multiple gives that meaning. The other options do not tell us how many babies there are. Choose C, multiple. Now read the sentence with the gap filled.

beats.action: Highlight proof sentence 15 and fill gap 25.
beats.label: Highlight proof sentence 15 and fill gap 25

lessons.syllabus: Read the passage closely and use its evidence to answer the question.
